title: Innovations in Smart Packaging Concepts for Food: An Extensive Review

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts, Scope, and Regulatory Framework
subsections.subsection_title: Core Concepts and Scope of Intelligent Packaging
subsections.content:
Intelligent packaging is generally understood as a packaging system that does more than passively contain and protect food: it acquires, stores, and communicates information relevant to product condition and handling. A foundational distinction is therefore between active packaging, which modifies the package environment to preserve food, and intelligent packaging, which monitors, records, traces, or signals changes so that actors across the supply chain can make better decisions ref [1]. This communication-centered interpretation has become central to subsequent food-packaging literature and helps delimit the concept from broader, inconsistently used labels such as “smart packaging” ref [1].

Within this scope, intelligent packaging encompasses data carriers and sensing/indicating elements. Data carriers such as barcodes and RFID support identification, traceability, and logistics visibility, whereas indicators and sensors—especially time–temperature indicators, gas indicators, and biosensors—provide condition-specific information related to freshness, abuse history, package integrity, or contamination risk ref [1]. Time–temperature indicators are among the most established examples because they translate cumulative thermal exposure into an interpretable response linked to quality loss in chilled and frozen foods ref [1], ref [2], ref [3]. Oxygen and carbon-dioxide indicators similarly extend package communication by revealing leakage, respiration changes, or spoilage-related headspace shifts ref [4], ref [5].

The practical scope of intelligent packaging therefore spans the entire food supply chain, from manufacturing and distribution to retail, domestic use, and recall management. Its value lies not only in sensing, but in coupling package-derived data with decision-support systems for safety assurance, shelf-life estimation, inventory rotation, and consumer guidance ref [1]. At the same time, intelligent packaging should be viewed as a system-level concept involving the food, package, external environment, and information infrastructure, rather than as a single label or sensor alone ref [1], ref [6]. This systems perspective is especially important as newer platforms integrate printed electronics, RFID-enabled sensing, and low-cost biosensing to move from simple indication toward connected, data-rich food packaging ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts, Scope, and Regulatory Framework
subsections.subsection_title: Regulatory Framework for Food-Contact Packaging Materials
subsections.content:
The regulatory framework for food-contact packaging is anchored in the principle that materials must not transfer constituents to food in quantities that endanger human health, unacceptably alter food composition, or impair organoleptic quality. In the European Union, this general requirement is established by Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004, while plastic food-contact materials are specifically governed by Commission Regulation (EU) No 10/2011, which defines the Union list of authorised substances, overall and specific migration limits, declaration-of-compliance requirements, and traceability obligations ref [1], ref [2]. For smart and intelligent packaging, these baseline rules are complemented by Regulation (EC) No 450/2009, which adds substance authorization, functional barrier, labeling, and information requirements specific to active and intelligent components ref [3].

A central regulatory concept is migration-based risk control. Regulation (EU) No 10/2011 applies substance-specific migration limits (SMLs), overall migration limits, compositional restrictions, and testing rules using food simulants and standardized contact conditions ref [2]. Subsequent EFSA review has further shown that substances lacking explicit SMLs may still warrant prioritization based on hazard, volatility, molecular size, and exposure potential, illustrating that authorization is not static but subject to re-evaluation as toxicological evidence evolves ref [4]. In practice, safety assessment also considers impurities, reaction products, and, where relevant, nanoforms, the latter requiring explicit case-by-case authorization rather than being covered automatically by conventional approvals ref [2], ref [5].

Beyond the EU, regulatory oversight follows comparable risk-based logic, although implemented through different legal instruments. In the United States, food-contact substances are regulated through the Food Contact Notification program under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, with migration and intended-use conditions playing a central role in market clearance ref [6], ref [7]. For smart packaging developers, the key compliance challenge is therefore dual: demonstrating functional performance while ensuring that indicators, scavengers, sensors, inks, adhesives, and embedded additives remain within food-contact safety limits across realistic storage and use scenarios. This makes early regulatory-by-design integration essential to successful translation from concept to commercialization ref [3], ref [5], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Active Packaging Systems for Food Preservation
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations and Market Overview of Active Food Packaging
subsections.content:
Active food packaging emerged from the limits of passive barrier materials and modified-atmosphere systems, particularly for minimally processed foods that remain vulnerable to oxidation, moisture imbalance, and microbial spoilage. In foundational terms, active packaging is designed to deliberately absorb or release substances into the package headspace or food-contact environment so as to extend shelf life or maintain quality, distinguishing it from conventional inert containment ref [2], ref [3], ref [4], ref [6]. This broad class includes scavenging systems for oxygen, carbon dioxide, ethylene, and water vapor, as well as releasing systems for antimicrobial, antioxidant, and flavor-active compounds ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

A central technological transition has been the shift from sachet-based formats toward polymer-integrated systems, coatings, labels, and multilayer structures. Polymer-based active packaging is especially attractive because permeability, release kinetics, and compatibility can be engineered for specific foods, although functionality must be balanced against migration, stability, sensory neutrality, and regulatory compliance ref [3], ref [4], ref [6]. The literature also stresses that performance is product-specific: active agents effective in model media may behave differently in real foods because of matrix interactions, headspace conditions, and storage temperature ref [2], ref [3].

From a market perspective, oxygen scavengers remain the most mature and commercially visible segment, followed by moisture-control systems, antimicrobial packaging, and ethylene management for produce ref [2], ref [4], ref [6], ref [6]. Market growth has been driven by demand for fresher foods, reduced preservative use, longer distribution chains, and greater sustainability, but adoption still varies regionally because of consumer acceptance, cost, processing integration, and legislation governing active food-contact materials ref [2], ref [6], ref [6]. Accordingly, current innovation is focused less on proof-of-concept alone and more on scalable, regulation-ready, food-specific active packaging platforms ref [2], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Active Packaging Systems for Food Preservation
subsections.content:
Gas and moisture scavenging systems are central active-packaging tools because they directly control the headspace species that accelerate oxidation, respiration, textural deterioration, and microbial instability. Oxygen scavengers remain the dominant commercial class, complementing passive barriers by removing residual oxygen introduced during filling or permeating through the pack over storage; this distinction between barrier and scavenging functions is emphasized in recent mechanistic analyses of oxygen-barrier packaging ref [6], ref [9].

For oxygen control, conventional sachet-based iron systems are widely used, but current research increasingly targets embedded or catalytic scavengers with faster kinetics and better integration into films. Palladium-based systems are especially notable because Pd catalyzes the reaction of hydrogen with residual oxygen to form water; oxygen-scavenging rate depends strongly on substrate chemistry, SiOx interlayers, and ultrathin Pd thickness, with optimized PET- or PLA-based coated films removing low oxygen levels within minutes under suitable modified atmospheres ref [5]. More broadly, active oxygen-barrier platforms include cobalt-catalyzed oxidizable polymers, ascorbate- and iron-based scavengers, and multilayer structures designed to balance scavenging rate, transparency, and recyclability ref [6], ref [9].

Gas scavenging in fresh produce packaging also includes ethylene removal, since even trace ethylene accelerates ripening and senescence. Ethylene scavengers operate through oxidation, adsorption, receptor blocking, or photocatalytic pathways; potassium permanganate on mineral supports remains common, while zeolites, activated carbon, TiO2, and Pd-containing systems offer higher selectivity or regenerability in some formats ref [8], ref [9]. By contrast, moisture scavengers regulate water activity and condensation using desiccants such as silica gel, clays, calcium oxide, or superabsorbent salts, thereby limiting sogginess, caking, and microbial growth, although their design must be matched carefully to the product’s required relative humidity rather than simply maximizing drying capacity ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Active Packaging Systems for Food Preservation
subsections.content:
Antimicrobial active packaging couples controlled microbial inhibition with the package interface, where contamination is often concentrated, and is therefore closely aligned with food biopreservation strategies based on natural preservatives and hurdle technology. Current systems can be grouped into migrating films that release active compounds to the food surface or headspace, and non-migrating materials in which the active moiety is immobilized on the polymer surface [1], ref [14], ref [15]. This distinction is important because efficacy depends not only on intrinsic antimicrobial potency, but also on release kinetics, food composition, and interfacial contact conditions [1], ref [15].

Among biopreservatives, bacteriocins—especially nisin—remain the most studied due to regulatory acceptance and activity against Gram-positive spoilage and pathogenic bacteria. Their incorporation into polyethylene, cellulose, protein, and biodegradable PLA-based matrices has shown meaningful inhibition of Listeria and related targets in meat, dairy, and liquid foods [1], ref [13], ref [14], ref [15]. Notably, nisin can retain substantial activity even after brief exposure to PLA-processing temperatures, although stability decreases at higher temperatures and in PLA/PEG blends, underscoring the need to match antimicrobial chemistry with polymer-processing windows [3]. Immobilization and adsorption approaches further improve persistence at the food-contact surface and support controlled biopreservation without excessive additive migration [4].

Natural antimicrobials beyond bacteriocins are increasingly used to broaden spectrum and consumer acceptance. Chitosan-based and gelatin-chitosan edible films, as well as films carrying essential oils such as garlic oil, can enhance inhibition of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus cereus, and Listeria monocytogenes, while film composition also governs mechanical performance and release behavior [6]. More broadly, active biopreservation platforms based on organic acids, plant extracts, enzymes, and antimicrobial biopolymers have shown promise, but translation still depends on balancing antimicrobial efficacy with sensory impact, material processability, regulatory compliance, and long-term stability in real foods rather than model media alone [1], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Active Packaging Systems for Food Preservation
subsections.content:
Antioxidant and bioactive compound-releasing packaging is designed to delay lipid oxidation and quality loss by incorporating natural radical scavengers or other protective molecules into the packaging matrix, coating, or an intermediate carrier that enables controlled migration toward the food surface. Recent reviews emphasize a clear shift from synthetic antioxidants toward plant-derived phenolics, vitamins, and spice-derived compounds because they can simultaneously improve oxidative stability and align with clean-label expectations ref [16], ref [8].

Among the most studied releasable antioxidants are quercetin, gallic acid, α-tocopherol, and resveratrol. Poly(vinyl alcohol) films containing gallic acid or quercetin showed high radical-scavenging activity together with measurable migration into food simulants, illustrating how phenolic loading can confer both active and, in some cases, freshness-indicating functions through color changes during storage ref [18]. In biodegradable poly(L-lactic acid), α-tocopherol and resveratrol lowered glass-transition and melting temperatures while preserving processability and adding UV-screening and antioxidant potential, although compositional tuning was needed to balance plasticization and stiffness ref [20].

A central challenge is not merely loading bioactives, but modulating their release. Carrier-assisted strategies have therefore gained traction. Supercritical adsorption of quercetin onto maize starch and calcium alginate aerogels produced porous antioxidant reservoirs with markedly slower release than free quercetin, supporting their use as active layers in multilayer packaging ref [19]. Likewise, mesoporous silica-enabled LDPE films containing quercetin and α-tocopherol achieved synergistic antioxidant performance while reducing α-tocopherol diffusivity and promoting quercetin release, demonstrating how nanostructured hosts can decouple loading from migration control ref [10]. Beyond isolated compounds, herbs and spices remain an important source of multifunctional bioactives for packaging because their polyphenols and essential-oil constituents can provide concurrent antioxidant and antimicrobial effects, though volatility, sensory impact, and release predictability still limit broader translation ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Active Packaging Systems for Food Preservation
subsections.subsection_title: Thermal-Regulating Packaging with Phase Change Materials
subsections.content:
Thermal-regulating active packaging uses phase change materials (PCMs) to buffer transient thermal shocks during storage and distribution, thereby complementing conventional active functions aimed at gas, moisture, or microbial control. In food systems, the central design principle is to exploit the latent heat of fusion of a PCM whose transition temperature matches the critical preservation window, so that heat is absorbed or released at nearly constant temperature during abuse events in the cold chain or retail handling ref [7], ref [8].

A major materials challenge is leakage-free integration of PCMs into packaging structures. Microencapsulation has therefore become a key enabling strategy, because shell materials physically isolate the core PCM, improve handling, and facilitate incorporation into films, panels, coatings, or inserts. Foundational work on microcapsule preparation established how interfacial conditions, shell formation, and surfactant selection govern capsule morphology and core retention ref [25]. More specifically for latent-heat storage, microencapsulated paraffin@SiO2 composites showed stable core-shell architectures, suppressed leakage above the melting point, and retained phase-transition behavior over repeated thermal cycles, illustrating why inorganic or hybrid shells are attractive for food-contact-adjacent applications requiring thermal robustness ref [5].

At the package scale, PCM integration can produce measurable thermal buffering. Packaging concepts containing microencapsulated octanoic-acid PCM prolonged thermal protection of chocolate relative to reference packs and outperformed the same PCM in bulk form, indicating that encapsulation can improve both safety and heat-buffering efficiency in compartmentalized designs ref [7]. Likewise, insulated cold-chain containers incorporating PCMs with melting points tuned near 5 °C maintained internal temperatures within the 2–8 °C range for more than 80 h under severe ambient conditions, whereas water-based PCM exhibited subcooling and inferior control ref [8]. These results highlight that PCM selection, transition temperature matching, encapsulation strategy, and package geometry jointly determine performance. Remaining barriers include limited latent-heat loading in polymeric matrices, cost, recyclability, and the need to validate migration and regulatory compliance for direct food-packaging deployment ref [5], ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Intelligent Packaging: Indicators, Sensors, and Monitoring Technologies
subsections.subsection_title: Concepts and Roles of Intelligent Packaging
subsections.content:
Intelligent packaging is generally defined as a packaging system that extends the communication function of the package beyond passive labeling, enabling the package to detect, record, trace, and transmit information relevant to food quality, safety, and handling conditions ref [26], ref [1], ref [27], ref [28]. In this sense, intelligence does not imply direct preservation action, as in active packaging, but rather the generation of decision-relevant information for manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and consumers ref [1], ref [28].

A central conceptual contribution in the literature is the view of intelligent packaging as part of a broader information and decision-support system. Because the package accompanies the product throughout the supply chain, it is uniquely positioned to monitor the food and its environment and to communicate status data visually or electronically ref [26], ref [1]. This systems perspective typically integrates smart package devices, data layers, data processing, and communication networks, thereby linking condition monitoring with traceability, logistics, and corrective action ref [26], ref [1].

Accordingly, the main roles of intelligent packaging in foods are: monitoring product history and storage conditions; indicating changes associated with spoilage, leakage, or abuse; supporting traceability and inventory management; and improving risk management in quality assurance and HACCP-type frameworks ref [26], ref [1], ref [27]. Typical intelligent elements include data carriers such as barcodes and RFID tags, and condition-monitoring tools such as time–temperature indicators, gas indicators, and biosensors ref [26], ref [1], ref [28]. Recent reviews also emphasize that intelligent packaging can strengthen consumer confidence and reduce waste by enabling more realistic freshness assessment than static date labels alone ref [27], ref [28].

From an implementation perspective, intelligent packaging has evolved alongside advances in sensors, printable electronics, low-cost labels, and wireless data exchange, making smart communication increasingly feasible in commercial food systems ref [26], ref [1], ref [28]. Nevertheless, its practical value depends on reliable calibration to food deterioration pathways, regulatory compliance, and user-friendly interpretation of the generated signals ref [26], ref [27]. These considerations frame the subsequent discussion of indicators, flexible sensors, and electrochemical and gas-sensing platforms for food monitoring.

subsections.section_title: Intelligent Packaging: Indicators, Sensors, and Monitoring Technologies
subsections.content:
Time–temperature indicators (TTIs) are among the earliest and most mature intelligent packaging tools for perishables because they integrate the cumulative thermal history of a product into an easily interpretable response, typically based on diffusion, polymerization, enzymatic, microbiological, or photochromic mechanisms ref [29]. Unlike a simple expiry date, TTIs better reflect cold-chain abuse during transport and storage, which is critical for foods whose quality loss is strongly temperature dependent, including meat, fish, dairy, and minimally processed produce ref [29]. Commercial systems such as Fresh-Check, MonitorMark, and Timestrip illustrate the practical value of irreversible visual labels, although calibration to specific food deterioration kinetics remains essential for reliable deployment ref [29].

Freshness indicators complement TTIs by responding to metabolites generated during spoilage, especially pH shifts and volatile basic nitrogen compounds. In protein-rich foods, microbial activity and biochemical degradation generate ammonia and amines, which can be transduced into visible color changes by pH-sensitive dyes embedded in films or labels ref [31], ref [5]. Natural anthocyanins have become particularly attractive because they are food-compatible pigments with broad pH-dependent chromatic transitions and can be sourced from red cabbage, butterfly pea, purple sweet potato, berries, and related plant matrices ref [32], ref [5]. Their structural interconversion among flavylium, quinoidal, and chalcone forms underlies the red-to-blue-to-green/yellow responses widely exploited in smart freshness labels ref [32], ref [5].

Recent work has therefore shifted toward biodegradable colorimetric indicators in which anthocyanins are immobilized in starch, chitosan, agar, carrageenan, or PVA-based supports. For example, a sago-based film incorporating butterfly pea anthocyanin showed clear color transitions with poultry spoilage, demonstrating low-cost real-time monitoring through pH-responsive visual change ref [31]. Related anthocyanin films have been reported as both freshness indicators and, in some formulations, as time–temperature indicators when the color evolution correlates with temperature-dependent degradation kinetics ref [30], ref [5]. Despite their promise, these systems still face challenges in pigment stability against light, oxygen, and heat, migration control, and quantitative standardization under real supply-chain conditions ref [29], ref [32].

subsections.section_title: Intelligent Packaging: Indicators, Sensors, and Monitoring Technologies
subsections.content:
Disposable and flexible sensor platforms are increasingly important in intelligent food packaging because they enable low-cost, single-use, and distributed monitoring without the cleaning, recalibration, or contamination issues associated with reusable devices. Their design typically separates a disposable sensing element from a reusable reader, which is particularly attractive for package-integrated food quality surveillance and point-of-need analysis ref [33].

Material selection is central to these platforms. Paper, cellulose derivatives, PET, polyimide, elastomers, and hybrid laminates support lightweight and conformable devices that can be fabricated by screen printing, inkjet printing, roll-to-roll coating, or transfer processes at high throughput ref [33]. For food packaging, flexible substrates also permit intimate contact with curved containers and thin headspace regions, improving responsiveness while minimizing package-volume penalties. Hybrid architectures that combine polymer supports with printed metals, carbon inks, or nanomaterials are especially attractive because they balance mechanical compliance, electrical conductivity, and low manufacturing cost ref [33].

A notable recent direction is the development of biodegradable flexible sensors that reduce electronic waste after use. Salvatore et al. reported ultrathin temperature sensors based on magnesium microstructures encapsulated in a compostable polymer, showing fast thermal response, stable operation under folding, crumpling, and stretching up to 10%, and wireless readout via a Bluetooth module ref [34]. Such transient or compostable platforms are highly relevant to cold-chain food packaging, where temperature tracking is essential but sensor recovery is often impractical. More broadly, biodegradable substrates and conductors align intelligent packaging with circular-economy goals by coupling sensing functionality with end-of-life sustainability ref [33], ref [34].

Despite this progress, disposable flexible platforms still face trade-offs among mechanical robustness, barrier compatibility, signal drift under humidity, and seamless integration with packaging converting lines. Future developments are likely to emphasize fully printed multimodal tags, battery-free or near-field-enabled readout, and substrate/electrode systems that are simultaneously food-safe, scalable, and environmentally benign ref [33], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Intelligent Packaging: Indicators, Sensors, and Monitoring Technologies
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical and Gas-Sensing Technologies for Food Monitoring
subsections.content:
Electrochemical and gas-sensing technologies extend intelligent packaging from passive indication to direct measurement of volatile spoilage markers, enabling earlier and more quantitative assessment of food quality. In food systems, ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide, biogenic amines, oxygen, and humidity are among the most informative targets because they track microbial activity, protein degradation, package integrity, and storage atmosphere. Compared with purely colorimetric labels, these platforms can offer lower detection limits, continuous readout, and easier integration with wireless or electronic packaging architectures [ref [36]].

A notable direction is the use of room-temperature transistor and electrochemical transduction for trace-gas analysis. Decorated silicon chemical-sensitive field-effect transistor arrays have demonstrated multiplexed detection of NH3, H2S, and humidity with reported limits down to 10 ppb, while maintaining low hysteresis and low cross-sensitivity; importantly, these arrays were validated during egg and pork spoilage tests, showing that multi-marker tracking can capture temperature-dependent spoilage onset in real time [ref [36]]. Such performance is significant because practical food monitoring requires not only sensitivity, but also simultaneous discrimination among chemically overlapping headspace components.

Optical gas sensing is also emerging as a complementary route for smart food packs. Silicon photonic microring resonators functionalized with acidic nanoporous aluminosilicate films have shown selective and reversible ammonia detection, with response equilibration in less than 30 s, recovery within about 60-90 s, and an estimated detection limit near 5 ppm, while exhibiting selectivity over CO2 [ref [3]]. Although optical platforms are less established in packaging than electrochemical labels, their CMOS-compatible fabrication, multiplexing potential, and ambient-temperature operation make them attractive for future integrated package monitoring nodes [ref [3]].

Overall, the main design challenge is balancing sensitivity, selectivity, reversibility, humidity tolerance, and cost in a form factor compatible with disposable food packaging. Current evidence suggests that multi-analyte arrays, rather than single-gas devices, are especially promising because spoilage signatures are matrix- and temperature-dependent. Future work should therefore emphasize calibration across food categories, antifouling and low-drift operation under humid headspaces, and scalable coupling of sensing elements with low-power readout electronics for truly deployable intelligent packaging systems [ref [36], ref [3]].

Traceability in smart food packaging increasingly relies on RFID because it enables non-line-of-sight identification, item- to pallet-level tracking, and dynamic association of package identity with logistics, processing, and environmental records ref [37]. In food chains, this capability is especially valuable for rapid recall execution, inventory synchronization, and verification of provenance across multiple handling nodes, where conventional barcodes remain limited by line-of-sight scanning and lower data capacity ref [37].

For food applications, RFID architectures span passive, semi-passive, and active tags, with frequency selection and package environment strongly affecting performance. Passive UHF systems are attractive for low-cost supply-chain deployment, whereas semi-passive or active formats are better suited when temperature logging or other sensing functions must be integrated into the package or transport unit ref [37]. However, implementation in foods is constrained by attenuation from water-rich products, detuning near metals, interoperability issues across standards, and persistent concerns about cost, recycling, privacy, and read reliability in dense retail environments ref [37].

An important specialized branch is surface acoustic wave (SAW)-based RFID, which offers a passive alternative with low interrogation power, meter-scale readout, and inherent compatibility with harsh environments and sensing functions such as temperature measurement ref [38]. SAW tags encode identity through delayed acoustic reflections rather than chip-based memory, and advances in time-position and phase encoding have expanded code capacity while preserving passive operation ref [38]. Although reader complexity and commercialization remain challenges, SAW-RFID is particularly relevant for food logistics where robust identification on metal surfaces, in cold chains, or under demanding processing conditions is required ref [38].

subsections.subsection_title: Sensor Information Acquisition in Industrial and Microfluidic Systems
subsections.content:
Sensor information acquisition in smart-packaging-related process lines increasingly relies on embedded or non-contact measurement architectures that can operate across both industrial equipment and miniaturized analytical platforms. In industrial settings, temperature, gas composition, humidity, and time–temperature history are typically captured through integrated resistive, optical, or disposable sensing formats, with the resulting data used for process control, cold-chain verification, and quality prediction ref [39], ref [2]. Complementary gas-sensing approaches based on silicon photonic resonators and transistor arrays further illustrate how high-sensitivity acquisition can be translated into compact interrogation systems suitable for food-quality monitoring and distributed analytical nodes ref [3], ref [4].

At the microfluidic scale, information acquisition becomes especially important because microscale heat and mass transfer strongly influence reaction kinetics, separations, and assay reliability. A notable advance is in situ luminescence thermometry using Er3+/Yb3+-doped NaYF4 nanoparticles, which enables ratiometric temperature readout directly inside microchannels rather than outside the device. Geitenbeek et al. demonstrated accurate internal measurements up to at least 120 °C with about 0.34 °C agreement relative to integrated platinum RTDs, while also enabling localized probing in silicon/glass, PDMS/glass, and glass/glass chips ref [5]. Because the method is ratiometric, it reduces concentration dependence that limits intensity-based dye thermometry, and it extends the usable range beyond many conventional fluorescent probes ref [5].

The same study also showed that acquisition modality can be adapted to the required spatial scale: fiber-optic interrogation provided millimeter-scale spot measurements for routine chip monitoring, whereas confocal acquisition reduced the effective spot size to around 9 µm, allowing reconstruction of imposed thermal gradients and exothermic mixing profiles within microchannels ref [5]. More broadly, such microfluidic sensing strategies are relevant to food packaging innovation because they support rapid formulation screening, migration studies, spoilage-metabolite analysis, and calibration of flexible indicators under controlled microscale environments. In this sense, industrial sensor networks and microfluidic acquisition platforms should be viewed as complementary layers in the digitalization of smart food packaging systems ref [39], ref [2], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Commercial Implementation of Flexible and Printed Sensing Technologies
subsections.content:
Commercial implementation of flexible and printed sensing technologies for food packaging is increasingly shaped by manufacturability rather than sensing performance alone. Printed electronics offers low-temperature, large-area fabrication on polymer films and paper-like substrates, with compatibility for disposable indicators, conductive traces, antennas, and hybrid sensor platforms relevant to smart packages ref [40]. Among the available routes, screen, inkjet, gravure, flexographic, aerosol-jet, and slot-die processes have emerged as the principal industrial options, each balancing resolution, ink viscosity window, throughput, and cost differently ref [40].

For market translation, roll-to-roll and sheet-fed production are especially important because food packaging demands very high volumes, low unit cost, and robust registration over multilayer stacks. The manufacturing literature emphasizes that scalable deployment depends on coordinated control of substrate handling, web tension, drying/sintering, ink rheology, and interlayer compatibility; otherwise yield losses rapidly offset the economic advantages of printed formats ref [40]. In practice, screen and flexographic printing remain attractive for thicker conductive features and labels, whereas inkjet and aerosol approaches are better suited to digital customization and rapid prototyping of sensing layouts ref [40].

Despite this promise, commercial uptake in food systems still faces persistent barriers: sensor drift over shelf life, sensitivity to humidity and mechanical deformation, migration and food-contact compliance, calibration under real logistics conditions, and integration with readable consumer or supply-chain interfaces. As a result, the most realistic near-term products are hybrid solutions in which printed conductive patterns, simple colorimetric elements, and RFID/NFC components are combined rather than fully replacing conventional electronics. Accordingly, the path to commercialization is likely to proceed through application-specific, low-cost architectures manufactured on mature printed-electronics lines and validated under packaging-relevant operating conditions ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Synthesis, and Supporting Illustrative Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Synthesis Strategies for Functional Biopolymer Films
subsections.content:
Synthesis of functional biopolymer films for smart and active food packaging generally follows three complementary routes: solvent casting, thermomechanical processing, and post-synthesis network modification. Solvent casting remains prevalent for chitosan, gelatin, alginate, and starch because it enables mild incorporation of pH-sensitive dyes, antioxidants, and antimicrobials, whereas extrusion or melt blending is more attractive for scale-up of thermoplastic starch and PLA-based systems [1, 2, 3, 4]. The choice of route strongly governs additive dispersion, residual solvent or moisture, and the final balance between transparency, flexibility, and barrier performance [5, 6].

For polysaccharide-rich matrices, formulation engineering is as important as the processing route. Plasticizers such as glycerol and sorbitol improve film continuity but often increase chain mobility, water uptake, and gas permeability, while cross-linking with citric acid or phenolic compounds can partially restore cohesion and reduce transport through the matrix [7, 8, 9]. In starch systems, thermal-mechanical processing may also induce chain scission and molecular rearrangement, so synthesis conditions must be tuned to avoid excessive depolymerization while preserving active functionality [1, 10]. A useful illustration is the incorporation of rice-straw phenolic extracts into starch by melt blending and compression molding, which yielded homogeneous antioxidant films with improved oxygen barrier properties, albeit with increasing brittleness at higher extract loadings because of stronger starch–phenolic interactions and reduced plasticization [1].

Current synthesis strategies therefore increasingly favor hybrid designs: multilayer architectures that decouple sensing from barrier roles, compatibilized biopolymer blends, and waste-derived functional additives that support circular packaging concepts [3, 4, 11, 12]. Compression molding, extrusion, and reactive blending are especially promising for translational manufacturing, but they require careful control of temperature history, water activity, and interfacial compatibility to maintain indicator response and active-agent stability [1, 6, 10]. In practice, successful film synthesis is less about a single material choice than about co-optimizing polymer chemistry, additive incorporation route, and process intensity.

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Synthesis, and Supporting Illustrative Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Encapsulation Approaches for Active Packaging Components
subsections.content:
Encapsulation is increasingly used to stabilize active packaging agents that are otherwise prone to volatilization, oxidation, thermal degradation, or rapid diffusion from the polymer matrix. This is particularly important for essential oils, bacteriocins, enzymes, phages, and other natural antimicrobials, for which sustained activity and reduced sensory impact are central design criteria. A recent update on antimicrobial packaging systems identifies encapsulation not merely as a protection step, but as a route to improve polymer compatibility, loading efficiency, and release control under realistic food-storage conditions ref [42].

Among current approaches, emulsions and nanoemulsions are widely adopted for dispersing hydrophobic actives in hydrophilic biopolymer films, often improving transparency, homogeneity, and antimicrobial efficacy relative to coarse dispersions ref [42]. Core-shell electrospun fibers further extend this concept by physically separating the active core from the shell, enabling slower release and better retention of volatile compounds ref [42]. Cyclodextrin inclusion complexes are also prominent because they enhance aqueous dispersibility and thermal stability of essential oils and other small hydrophobes, while halloysite nanotubes provide an inexpensive inorganic carrier with high loading capacity and delayed diffusion profiles ref [42].

Liposomes, nanocapsules, and polymeric nanoparticles broaden the design space by accommodating both hydrophilic and lipophilic agents and, in some cases, enabling trigger-responsive release. Nevertheless, these systems also introduce trade-offs, including opacity changes, added formulation complexity, migration assessment requirements, and scale-up costs. Overall, the field is moving from simple agent incorporation toward structurally engineered delivery platforms, where the encapsulation architecture is selected together with the film matrix to match the target food, release kinetics, and regulatory constraints ref [42].
